title: Playing with violinist Cyune, Johnny Bynum and bassist Jose
summary: After August, Nash played with Baton Rouge violinist Cyune, Johnny Bynum and Frank Wagner, with bassist Jose now in Los Angeles.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Let's see, after you worked with August, who did you work with?

Well, after I worked with August, I worked with Cyun, a violin player. He's an old timer too. He lived in Baton Rouge, you know. We used to play all out of the canal in front, that Eddie Woodruff place. You know where he is? Walter Coren, the one that had the position in the custom house. We used to play for all their parties. They used to throw on big parties. There's La Youn, the violin player. He lived in Baton Rouge.
What part of Baton Rouge does he live in?

I can go right to his house, but I couldn't tell you. Some of the streets I know in Baton Rouge, like Alabama Street, Louisa Street, East Boulevard, Highland Road, and Floyd Street. I know where that's at. Then they got another street in Baton Rouge I know too. They had Posey Street in Baton Rouge. Then they had, at that time they had another street in Baton Rouge called, what street is that? Cozy, Posey Street. Then they had, I can't think of the name of that street.
Does he live around Scotlandville or close in than that?

No, he don't live very far from Louisa Street. It's a fella got a place out there in Baton Rouge they call the APEC. It's a ballroom. Anybody in that APEC that you ever catch in the APEC going to show you where Sa Youn lives. Sa Youn don't live far from that. Well he's one of the old violin players of New Orleans. We all played together. He played violin. We had a violin, ukulele, and I had another boy who played a mandolin with me, Johnny Bynum. He died in Baton Rouge. He and I traveled all over together playing. I was playing guitar then. We had a guitar and mandolin. We had a fella play bass we met in Nashville, Tennessee. But he finally came to the bad news and he died. He died here about, Johnny been dead now two years ago. I met a fella on canal in Rampart. Told me, say, you know Johnny play, a fella played beautiful mandolin. You and him used to play this? He said, yeah. He said, they just buried him last week. I mean, about two years ago. Let me see now.
Let me turn it off a second. You tell him about you played with Sa Youn and Bynum was with you? Mm-hmm. And all that, okay? Yeah. And then what happened?

Well, me and Sa Youn, Frank Wagner, we was the lady that had a Jose. Jose. Jose played bass with us. That's right. He's in California now, Los Angeles. He's an old timer. Oh, he must be about, Jose about 70. Jose 50, 60, 70. Jose must be about 88 years old now, but he's still playing the bass.
Jose's still playing the bass out there?
That's right, in California. That's right. He left here and went to Los Angeles.
All I know is Jose. I can't think of that other name.

Well, I'd love to find an 88 year old bass player. Yeah. What part of California? Los Angeles. Los Angeles, yeah. That's right. Well, we'll find him, somehow. Johnny St. Seah ought to know where he is. I bet you they know each other.
Johnny's in Los Angeles too, yeah. I bet Johnny, I know Johnny doesn't found him since he's been out there. I'm sure he is. That would be great.
We can find him too, man. You know more people all over. Yeah. I got a fella right now, play bass with me.

He's 80 some years old. He's 88. I mean, play much rhythm as you want to hear. Papa John. We've been practicing last week. Remember, I got a nice little set up now, full pieces. John Joseph. Yeah, that's right. They call him Papa John.

You know him, huh? Well, sure. Well, he's 88, I heard. I heard he's 88. He's 88. Well, he changes his age from day to day. But he's gotta be up in his 80s or 90s. Yeah, he's a hundred and a hundred. Well, let's see.
